incidents.inputs: A new preflight script whose whole purpose is to read a project's incident register before delivery, and an outside workshop that had translated the kit's folder names into its own language.
incidents.error: The register path was hardcoded to source/quality/incidents.json. On that workshop the script announced 'this project has logged no incidents yet' over a register holding 109 of them, and its checklist silently dropped every lesson that workshop had already paid for.
incidents.why: Two defects stacked. The path was assumed rather than resolved, and — worse — a failure to READ the file was rendered with the same sentence as a file that was read and found empty. 'Nothing to do' and 'nothing seen' produce the same value, and only one of them is good news. The script reproduced, on its first outside run, the exact failure family it was built to catch.
incidents.generic: A tool that reads a project's data must resolve that path rather than assume it, and must never render 'could not read the input' with the same words as 'read the input, it was empty'. A check that reports all-clear when it simply failed to find its input is worse than no check at all.

incidents.inputs: A plain-text email draft for a real recipient, already composed and hard-wrapped, a few lines slightly over the target width.
incidents.error: Ran a script to rewrap it to 78 columns. The script treated each already-wrapped line as a paragraph, so it re-broke every one: orphan words, a hyphenated word split across two lines, and the two-line sign-off folded into one. Done again on a second draft in the same session before the pattern was recognised.
incidents.why: The rewrapper's input model was wrong and untested: it assumed unwrapped paragraphs and got wrapped lines. Reaching for a script felt cheaper than retyping, and the damage was only visible on reading the whole output, which the first run did not do.
incidents.generic: Compose a plain-text message at its final line width from the start. Never post-process the wrapping of prose that is already wrapped: the tool cannot see paragraphs, only lines, and it will break words and collapse structure.

incidents.inputs: A daily scheduled sweep whose own instructions name the Gmail connector as the only path to the work mailbox, and a machine with two Chrome profiles connected, one signed into the work account and one into the owner's personal account.
incidents.error: A funding sweep read the owner's personal mailbox instead of the work one it is scoped to.
incidents.why: A routine decommissioned on 2026-08-26 kept its instruction file on disk, unregistered but runnable. That file asserts 'There is no Gmail MCP connector' (false since the connector was added) and tells the agent to drive the owner's logged-in Chrome at /mail/u/0/, which resolves to whichever account is default in whichever profile it reaches. The playbook that supersedes it was updated correctly; the executable copy of the old instructions was not removed. FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG: this was initially attributed to a silent browser fallback inside the daily drain, on the strength of that task's description mentioning funding, without checking whether a task by the literal name existed. It did.

guard.where: the decommissioned file now opens with a hard stop; docs/failure-modes.md §4; memory two-gmail-accounts

incidents.generic: When a routine is retired, delete or cap its instruction file in the same change as the decision. A superseded playbook is a stale sentence; a superseded automation left on disk is a stale sentence something can still execute, and it will assert facts that were true when written. Also: a task's description is not its identity — check whether a routine by the literal name exists before attributing behaviour to a different one.

incidents.inputs: check-fleet.mjs, which answers how far behind the template each instance in a workspace is. The update-kit skill instructs the owner to run it from their own project, not from the template.
incidents.error: Run from anywhere but the template, every 'N template commit(s) behind' is wrong, and the closing alert fires on it. `const templateHead = await git(ROOT, ['rev-parse','HEAD'])` with ROOT = process.cwd() takes the CALLING repo's head as the template's, so `sha..templateHead` counts the project's own commits since it last synced. Reproduced here: run from the template, huguescharnallet is 12 behind and personal-paul up to date; run from huguescharnallet, the same scan says 189 behind and 'no template HEAD to compare' for the up-to-date one — the second symptom the report had not seen, since an instance whose sha is not in the caller's history cannot be ranged at all.

guard.where: scripts/test-check-fleet.mjs — the behind count must be identical run from the template and from a project; verified failing on the pre-fix script. The template is located by its origin, and an ungrounded figure is refused rather than printed.

incidents.generic: A script that compares against a reference must locate that reference, never assume it is where it was started. The failure is silent in the worst way: the number is plausible, it moves in the right direction as work accumulates, and it grows with the project's own activity — so the more an instance is worked, the more urgently it claims to be out of date.

incidents.inputs: The SessionStart hook that announces kit news, registered in .claude/settings.json, and check-fleet's second question: is this instance WIRED to tell its own owner anything?
incidents.error: An instance can report 'news: wired' while the mechanism has never once run. The hook's command is `node "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/scripts/kit-news.mjs" 2>/dev/null || true`, so on a machine with no node it fails silently and succeeds loudly. check-fleet reads the hook's presence in settings.json and calls that wired. An outside user ran a month of sessions this way and found it only when a diagnostic prompt made him install node.

guard.where: kit-news writes .git/kit-news-ran on every run before any early exit; check-fleet reports 'configured' and 'ran' as different answers, and says outright that the receipt only exists from 2026-08-31 so an absence proves nothing yet.

incidents.generic: This is the kit's own rule about safeguards, applied to the kit: a check that never fires leaves no trace, so its silence proves nothing. `2>/dev/null || true` on a notifier converts every failure into a positive claim. A tool that reports on a mechanism must test the mechanism, not read its configuration — the configuration is what someone intended, not what happens.

incidents.inputs: check-fleet.mjs reads each instance's working copy on disk — .kit-sync, .claude/settings.json — to answer whether it is wired and how far behind it is.
incidents.error: An outside user's scan reported that a project had neither the hook nor .kit-sync, and he wrote to say so. Both were on origin/main and had been for days; his local clone was 118 commits old. He caught it himself before acting, but the report he nearly acted on said a healthy repo needed repair.

guard.where: check-fleet prints each clone's lag against its own origin above every verdict drawn from it, and the template clone's own lag above the whole report; covered by a test.

incidents.generic: A tool that inspects a working copy is answering a question about a checkout, not about a project, and it must say which. Reporting 'NOT WIRED' from a stale clone is the silent-expiry family aimed at the maintainer: the sentence was true of what was on disk and false of the thing the reader cares about. State the age of the evidence next to the verdict drawn from it.

incidents.inputs: error-report.mjs turns source/quality/incidents.json into the report a project sends its maintainer. Its headline figure is how many incidents produced an executable guard rather than a written rule.
incidents.error: The count of unguarded incidents matched only guard.kind 'none', while the sentence printing it read 'produced nothing but a written rule', so every 'rule' entry landed in neither population. The register had also grown two kinds the schema never listed, 'test' and 'tool', and nothing rejected them, so those vanished from every total too. On this repo's own register the output was '1 produced an executable check; 0 produced nothing but a written rule' over six incidents: five uncounted, and the one figure that says whether the framework is improving read as perfect coverage. The detector map had the same hole: 'outside user' was not in it, so three incidents caught by a person were scored as if the framework had caught them, 2 of 6 instead of 5 of 6.
incidents.why: The buckets were written as independent filters rather than as a partition, so nothing forced them to add up to the total, and an unrecognised value could only ever fall out silently. Both fields are small closed enums that nothing validated.

guard.where: scripts/error-report.mjs — the four guard populations are a partition and the script exits non-zero rather than print a figure that does not add up; an unclassified kind is named in the report instead of dropped

incidents.generic: A metric built as several independent filters must be checked as a partition: assert the populations sum to the total and refuse to print if they do not. Any figure read off a closed enum needs that enum validated, because an unlisted value can only fail in the flattering direction. And the failure is worst in a document whose purpose is to stop someone reassuring themselves, so a self-assessment tool is where this assertion is least optional.

incidents.inputs: check-fleet.mjs walks the workspace and reports which repos run the framework, how far behind each is, and whether each is wired to announce a kit update.
incidents.error: It counted every repo whose CLAUDE.md merely named the framework as a full instance, and reported ten repos as permanently unwired. Those repos were satellites of a router, which is the architecture the framework's own guide prescribes for an organization of several repos, and in which a satellite deliberately carries none of the method. Obeying the report meant installing eleven copies of a framework that exists once. The owner refused it and wrote to explain why she had.
incidents.why: The tool encoded one of the two shapes the documentation describes, and asserted a verdict about repos it had no way to classify. Nobody had connected the guide to the script, and the map already held the information the script needed.

guard.where: scripts/check-fleet.mjs reads the Kind column of the ORGANIGRAM repo table, derives it only when the column is absent and says so; three cases in scripts/test-check-fleet.mjs, including that a repo declared a router is still held to every requirement

incidents.generic: When a guide describes more than one legal architecture, every tool that judges repos has to know which one it is looking at, and the map is where it reads that rather than guessing. An alarm that cannot be cleared without breaking the prescribed architecture stops being read, and takes the real alarms with it. Where a classification is derived rather than declared, say so in the output: the dangerous direction is a real instance quietly excused from every requirement.

incidents.inputs: A repo whose .gitignore forbids a file pattern, and files matching that pattern that were committed before the rule was added.
incidents.error: Four files of a financial model were tracked under a rule that forbade exactly them. An ignore rule applies only to files git is not already tracking, so the rule changed nothing, kept committing them on every change, and read as a guarantee. Reported by an outside user; nothing in the framework asked the question.
incidents.why: Adding the rule feels like the act of protection, so nobody checks the state it was supposed to create. The framework told owners to add ignore rules for sensitive material and never told them the rule is retroactive about nothing.

guard.where: scripts/check-freshness.mjs ▸ pass `ignored` — git check-ignore --no-index over every tracked file, naming the rule and the files that contradict it

incidents.generic: A safeguard added after the situation it was meant to prevent has to be verified against the current state, not assumed from the act of adding it. For an ignore rule specifically: untracking keeps the file on disk but does not remove it from history already pushed, so a credential that was in there must be changed rather than hidden.

incidents.inputs: Two owners asked to have a week of uncommitted work put somewhere safe before upgrading the framework.
incidents.error: The ordinary stash-and-branch path saves changes to files already tracked and silently ignores files never added, which on both machines were most of the week's output. One capture had to be redone; five documents would otherwise have gone, and the operation would have reported success either way.
incidents.why: The tool's definition of 'everything' is not the owner's, and the success message is written against the tool's definition.

guard.where: docs/failure-modes.md ▸ 5 · Before you destroy — enumerate untracked files, save them explicitly, then re-read the tree and confirm it is clean for the reason you think

incidents.generic: Before a rescue, enumerate what exists rather than trusting the tool's notion of what counts, and confirm afterwards that the tree is clean for the reason you believe. Where several sessions may be writing at once, take the capture without touching any working tree, since the tidy-up half of a stash is itself a write.

incidents.inputs: A new check written the same day to answer whether a repo's ignore rules are true, gated on finding a .gitignore in the directory walk the script already had.
incidents.error: That walk skips dotfiles, so the check reported 'no ignore rules to check' on a repo holding a forty-line .gitignore, and could never have fired anywhere. Caught by calibrating it on a repo built to fail, before it was committed.
incidents.why: The gate reused a helper written for a different purpose without checking what that helper excludes. A check that cannot fire produces exactly the output of a clean repo.

guard.where: docs/failure-modes.md ▸ 7 — calibrate a new check on a case known to be positive before trusting a silence; the comment in check-freshness.mjs records why the gate is gone

incidents.generic: A new check is not in place until it has been seen to fire once. Its silence and a clean result are the same output, so calibrate on a known positive first; and be suspicious of gating a check on a helper written for another purpose, since what that helper excludes is invisible at the call site.

incidents.inputs: An outside user's emailed report that ten of her repos were satellites of a router and that the fleet scan was wrong to demand the framework of them.
incidents.error: The assessment written for the owner, and the reply drafted to her, both stated flatly that she was right and the tool was wrong. Two halves of that were verified by reading the repo: the scan did classify on a CLAUDE.md substring, and the guide does prescribe router plus thin repos. The third was not: that her ten repos actually are thin repos. That came from her description and no one opened them. The owner challenged the claim before the reply was sent, which is the only reason it did not go out asserted.
incidents.why: An outside report arrives already argued, with its own evidence, and reads as a finding rather than as a claim to check. Verifying two of three premises produced the confidence of having verified the conclusion. The fix in code was also written as though her diagnosis had been confirmed end to end, so the guard now exempts a satellite from every requirement on the strength of a classification nobody validated.

guard.where: scripts/check-fleet.mjs prints when a kind is derived rather than read from the map, and scripts/test-check-fleet.mjs asserts a declared router is still held to every requirement — so a wrong classification is visible instead of silent

incidents.generic: An outside report is an input to verify, not a finding to adopt. Separate, in writing and before acting, what you confirmed yourself from what you took from the reporter, and say which is which when you answer them. Verifying most of the premises does not verify the conclusion. And when a fix relaxes a check on the strength of a classification, make the classification itself visible in the output: the dangerous direction is a real case quietly exempted, because an exemption produces no signal.

incidents.inputs: Sending two long plain-text emails through a browser-driven mail client, by focusing the compose body and issuing a synthetic type action.
incidents.error: The first mail typed correctly. The second dropped every ASCII character and kept only the accented ones, producing 425 characters of vowel salad in place of a 10 000-character letter. A synthetic paste had already failed silently before that, because a synthetic key event cannot read the clipboard. Nothing errored in either case: both reported success. Caught by reading back the field rather than trusting the action's own report.
incidents.why: Synthetic keystrokes are an unreliable transport for text of any length, and their failure mode is partial rather than absent, which is the mode that gets sent. The owner's instruction afterwards was categorical: never keystrokes.

guard.where: memory: browser text entry uses document.execCommand('insertText'), never synthetic typing or paste; and read the field back before any irreversible click

incidents.generic: Do not enter text into a web form with synthetic keystrokes or a synthetic paste. Use a DOM insertion command, and read the field back and compare its length and its ends before clicking anything irreversible. A URL parameter is not a fallback for long content either: the endpoint may simply answer Bad Request. Every one of these failures reported success.
